topics.title: Trump’s Peace Board
bullets: On January 22, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump inaugurated a Board of Peace to oversee and support the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.
The Board’s main role is to monitor compliance, facilitate communication between parties, etc.
The move signals renewed U.S. diplomatic involvement aimed at stabilising the region and sustaining the fragile ceasefire. Gaza –
Gaza is the main city and urban center of the Gaza Strip, a coastal territory in southwestern Palestine along the Mediterranean Sea, northeast of the Sinai Peninsula.
The Gaza Strip covers 140 square miles (363 square km) and is one of the most densely populated areas in the world.
It is unique because it is not legally recognized (de jure) as part of any existing sovereign country.
The first reliable census, in September 1967, showed a smaller population than earlier estimates by UNRWA or Egypt.
Nearly half of the population then lived in refugee camps. The population was 1,899,291 in 2017 and estimated at 2,226,544 in 2023.
In 2023, the population density was about 15,609 people per square mile (or 6,024 per square km). Timeline for Gaza-Israel conflict –
1949–1956 & 1957–1967: Gaza Strip was under Egyptian military rule but Egypt did not annex it or grant citizenship to Palestinian refugees living there in poor conditions.
Refugees couldn't migrate to Egypt or other Arab countries and were supported by UNRWA. Many young refugees became fedayeen (guerrillas) attacking Israel.
1956 (Suez Crisis): After attacks from Gaza, Israel invaded the Gaza Strip during the Sinai campaign. However, in 1957, international pressure forced Israel to return the territory to Egypt.
June 1967 (Six-Day War): Israel again occupied the Gaza Strip. This began a 25-year Israeli military presence.
December 1987: Widespread riots and clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinians marked the beginning of the first intifada (uprising).

1994: Under the Oslo Accords, Israel started transferring limited authority to the Palestinian Authority (PA), led by Yasser Arafat. However, the PA struggled with economic issues, limited support, and violent opposition from Hamas and Islamic Jihad.
Late 2000: Peace talks broke down, leading to the second intifada (Aqṣā intifada)—a more violent phase of conflict.

Late 2003: Israeli PM Ariel Sharon proposed withdrawal from Gaza. September 2005: Israel completed its military and settler withdrawal, transferring control to the PA. However, it still controlled Gaza's borders, airspace, and coast. Egypt patrolled the Philadelphi Corridor.
2007: After Hamas took over Gaza from the PA, Israel declared the strip a “hostile entity” and imposed sanctions, including power cuts and border restrictions.
January 2008: Hamas breached the Gaza–Egypt barrier, temporarily allowing Gazans to access supplies in Egypt.
August 2008: The Free Gaza Movement sent two boats with activists and medical supplies, breaching the blockade. Four more missions followed.
May 2011: Post-Mubarak Egypt reopened the Rafah border for daily movement of about 1,200 people, excluding trade.
2013: After Egyptian President Morsi was ousted, border traffic was reduced to 50 people/day, then closed due to security concerns.

Late 2017: PA regained control of Rafah border crossing. May 2018: Egypt allowed 200 people/day to cross. January 2019: After PA withdrew from Gaza, Hamas reopened the crossing. Thousands emigrated permanently during this time.
2018–2019: In an effort to reduce tensions, Israel allowed more goods in and expanded Gaza’s fishing zone. Thousands of Gazans were allowed to work in Israel.
End of 2018–2021: Qatar provided nearly $400 million in aid to Gaza with Israel and Egypt’s approval.
May 2021: Rising tensions in Jerusalem over Sheikh Jarrah evictions and Al-Aqsa clashes led Hamas to launch rockets. Israel responded with heavy air strikes.

October 7, 2023: Hamas launched a massive surprise land, sea, and air assault on Israel, killing 1,200+ people and taking ~240 hostages. It was Israel’s deadliest day since 1948. Israel declared war the next day and began a heavy offensive in Gaza. What is the Board of Peace?
Trump first proposed the Board of Peace in September as part of the second phase of the US-brokered 20-point Gaza ceasefire plan.
In November, the UN Security Council backed the plan, giving it international legitimacy and authorising the board to oversee demilitarisation and reconstruction of Gaza.

A draft charter obtained by CNN describes the Board of Peace as an international organisation aimed at promoting stability, peace and governance in regions affected or threatened by conflict — not limited to Gaza.
The charter states that Donald Trump will serve as chairman indefinitely, potentially beyond his second presidential term.
The Board of Peace will sit above a “founding Executive Board”, giving it overarching authority.
The Executive Board includes Jared Kushner, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, special envoy Steve Witkoff, and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair.
A core condition of the plan is Hamas’s demilitarisation, which Kushner said the US will enforce, though no enforcement mechanism was specified.
Presentation slides at Davos showed futuristic imagery — high-rise buildings, new roads, and modern energy infrastructure — outlining a radical redevelopment vision for Gaza.
Trump has suggested that the Board of Peace could potentially replace the United Nations in overseeing Gaza’s reconstruction and governance. Eligibility for the Peace Board –
Eligibility for joining Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) is defined strictly by its charter and varies by level of involvement.
Membership is invitation-only for countries and depends entirely on a personal invitation from Donald Trump, who can withdraw invitations at any time, including via social media.
Permanent membership for states requires a minimum $1 billion cash contribution to the BoP fund within the first year of the charter coming into force.
Countries that do not pay the $1 billion fee may receive a three-year membership, but renewal is solely at Trump’s discretion.
Each member state must be represented on the board by its Head of State or Head of Government.
The Executive Board is a smaller body handling day-to-day operations and global conflict resolution mandates.
Executive Board members are personally selected by the chairman, with no external approval process.
The charter requires Executive Board members to be “leaders of global stature.”
Current Executive Board members include senior diplomats (Marco Rubio), international mediators (Tony Blair, Nickolay Mladenov), and major business or financial figures (Ajay Banga, Marc Rowan).
Executive Board members serve two-year terms, which are renewable at the chairman’s discretion and can be terminated by him at any time.
Donald Trump is the inaugural chairman of the Board of Peace. The chairmanship is held indefinitely and ends only through voluntary resignation or incapacitation.
The chairman holds absolute veto power over membership invitations, renewals, and all board decisions, making the role dominant within the organisation. Members of the board –

Countries that have accepted Trump’s invitation include the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Bahrain, Pakistan, Turkey, Hungary, Morocco, Kosovo, Albania, Bulgaria, Argentina, and Paraguay.
Central Asian participants are Kazakhstan, Mongolia, and Uzbekistan, while Southeast Asian nations joining are Indonesia and Vietnam.

Israel has agreed to participate, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu supporting the initiative, despite his anger over the inclusion of Turkey and Qatar on the Gaza Executive Board and despite facing an International Criminal Court arrest warrant.
No Israeli representative appeared on stage at the Board of Peace ceremony; although President Isaac Herzog was in Davos, Netanyahu did not attend.
Armenia and Azerbaijan have also agreed to participate, following a US-brokered peace agreement last year that granted the US exclusive development access to a key regional transit corridor.
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has signed up, despite his reputation as Europe’s last dictator and his close alliance with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump claimed that Vladimir Putin has agreed to join, though Russia has not officially confirmed participation.

Putin has suggested using Russian assets frozen in the US to pay the $1 billion fee required for permanent membership, raising concerns about allowing a state actively engaged in war to sit on a peace body.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney initially planned to join with conditions, but Trump later rescinded Canada’s invitation.
Countries that have declined or raised objections include Britain, which refused to sign due to concerns about Russian involvement.
France and Norway declined, citing concerns over how the Board of Peace would function alongside the United Nations.
China confirmed it was invited but has not committed, stating it remains firmly committed to an international system with the UN at its core.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it was difficult to sit “together with Russia in any council,” calling Russia Ukraine’s enemy and Belarus its ally.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni declined to attend the signing ceremony, citing possible constitutional issues with joining.

topics.title: Ukraine Peace Talks
bullets: Peace talks between Russia and Ukraine were held in Abu Dhabi with the objective of exploring possibilities for de-escalation and conflict resolution.
The talks concluded without any significant breakthrough, particularly on the issue of the Donbas region, which remains the core area of dispute.
Both sides failed to reach a consensus on territorial claims, security guarantees, and ceasefire arrangements. Background of The Conflict:
The conflict between Russia and Ukraine escalated in February 2022 following Russia’s military invasion of Ukraine.
Tensions have their roots in Ukraine’s growing alignment with Western countries, particularly its aspirations to join NATO and the European Union.
Russia has consistently expressed security concerns over NATO’s eastward expansion near its borders.
The Donbas region, comprising Donetsk and Luhansk, has been a conflict zone since 2014, after pro-Russian separatist movements emerged.
Russia later recognized Donetsk and Luhansk as independent entities, a move rejected by Ukraine and most of the international community.
Several rounds of peace talks and mediation efforts have been attempted since 2022, but none have resulted in a lasting ceasefire.
The prolonged conflict has caused large-scale humanitarian crisis, displacement of civilians, and damage to critical infrastructure.
The war has also had global repercussions, impacting energy supplies, food security, and international geopolitics. About the Abu Dhabi Talks
The discussions were aimed at exploring possibilities for de- escalation and diplomatic resolution of the ongoing conflict.
These two-day negotiations were highly significant as they marked the first formal trilateral engagement between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine since the full-scale war began in early 2022.
The talks focused on key issues such as territorial disputes, security arrangements, and humanitarian concerns.
The Donbas region remained the central point of disagreement during negotiations.
No formal agreement or ceasefire announcement emerged from the talks.
Both sides described the discussions as constructive, despite the absence of tangible outcomes.
It was agreed that dialogue would continue through future diplomatic engagements. Key Outcomes of Abu Dhabi Talks
Russia and Ukraine agreed to hold a second round of direct talks, facilitated by the United States, in Abu Dhabi on 1 February 2026.
The talks were described as “constructive” and “positive” by Ukrainian and U.S. officials, indicating continued diplomatic engagement.
Discussions focused on military-related issues, with both sides identifying areas to be taken forward in subsequent talks.
Negotiations explored the broad parameters for ending the conflict, including security arrangements and post-conflict recovery.
Ukraine emphasized the need for U.S. monitoring and security guarantees to ensure effective implementation of any future agreement.
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant issue was discussed, however, control and operational arrangements remain unresolved.
Territorial questions, particularly concerning the Donbas, continue to be the primary point of deadlock between the two sides. Why Donbas is the Main Sticking Point?
The Donbas region includes the industrial areas of Donetsk and Luhansk, making it strategically and economically significant.
The region has been affected by armed conflict since 2014, leading to prolonged instability and competing territorial claims.
Russia considers Donbas critical for its security interests and has demanded Ukraine’s withdrawal from the region.
Ukraine maintains that Donbas is an integral part of its sovereign territory under international law.
The presence of Russian-backed forces and ongoing military activity complicates any political settlement Role of the United Arab Emirates
The United Arab Emirates hosted the peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, providing a neutral and non-aligned diplomatic platform.
By hosting the talks, the UAE facilitated trilateral engagement involving officials from the United States, Russia, and Ukraine, enabling direct diplomatic interaction.
The UAE provided the logistical and diplomatic framework necessary for high-level discussions on conflict de-escalation and peace parameters.
The talks included discussions on elements of a U.S.-proposed peace framework, covering security arrangements and post- conflict considerations.
Following the initial round, Abu Dhabi was confirmed as the venue for the next round of negotiations scheduled for early February 2026.
Russia and Ukraine acknowledged the UAE’s role in facilitating dialogue and maintaining diplomatic channels amid ongoing hostilities. Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is Europe’s largest nuclear power facility, located in southern Ukraine.
The plant has been under de facto Russian control since March 2022 and is managed by a subsidiary of Rosatom, though it is internationally recognized as Ukrainian property under Energoatom.
The facility is currently in a shutdown state and is not supplying electricity to the grid, relying on external power lines for critical cooling systems.
The issue featured prominently during the Abu Dhabi talks, with discussions focusing on future oversight, safety, and economic output of the plant.
While no agreement on control was reached, proposals included joint or trilateral management frameworks and equitable sharing of electricity output once operations resume.
The International Atomic Energy Agency continues to maintain a presence at the site and has facilitated limited safety arrangements to enable essential repairs.
